stem: Which keyword is used in Java to inherit from a class?

options.text: implements
inherits
extends
super

explanation: A class uses `extends` to inherit from a class. `implements` is used for interfaces.

stem: Which block always runs, whether or not an exception is thrown?

options.text: catch
try
throws
finally

explanation: `finally` runs after try/catch regardless of the outcome, which makes it suitable for cleanup.

stem: A class can directly extend how many classes in Java?

options.text: One
Two
Any number
None

explanation: Java has single class inheritance. A class may implement many interfaces.

stem: `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();` calls which version of `speak`?

options.text: Animal's version, because the variable type is Animal
Dog's overriding version, chosen at runtime
It does not compile because Animal cannot hold a Dog
Whichever method is declared first in the source file

explanation: Overridden instance methods use dynamic dispatch, so the runtime type (Dog) decides.

stem: Which of these is a checked exception?

options.text: NullPointerException
IllegalArgumentException
IOException
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

explanation: Checked exceptions such as IOException must be caught or declared. The others are unchecked runtime exceptions.

stem: When is an abstract class a better choice than an interface?

options.text: When a class must inherit from several parents at once
When the type should declare no methods or fields at all
When the class must be final and can never be extended
When subclasses should share state or common implemented code

explanation: Abstract classes can hold instance fields and shared constructors or logic. Interfaces define a contract without instance state.

stem: Which collection does NOT allow duplicate elements?

options.text: ArrayList
HashSet
LinkedList
Vector

explanation: A Set stores unique elements. Lists allow duplicates.

stem: Which structure stores key-value pairs?

options.text: ArrayList
HashSet
HashMap
ArrayDeque

explanation: `HashMap` maps keys to values.

stem: What is the average time complexity of `get` on a `HashMap`?

options.text: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)

explanation: Hashing gives constant-time average lookups, degrading only with heavy collisions.

stem: What does `List<? extends Number>` accept?

options.text: A list of Number or any subclass such as Integer, for reading
Only a List<Number>, never a list of a subclass such as Integer
A list of any type at all, including String and Object
Only lists whose element type is exactly Object

explanation: An upper-bounded wildcard accepts lists of Number or its subtypes. You can read Numbers but cannot safely add.

stem: To sort a `List<Person>` by age descending, which is correct?

options.text: list.sort(Person::getAge) which sorts descending by default
list.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::getAge).reversed())
Collections.sort(list, -1) using -1 to request descending order
list.sort(null).reverse() to sort naturally then flip the list

explanation: `Comparator.comparingInt(...).reversed()` builds a comparator for descending age.

stem: Why can you not create `new T()` or `new T[10]` inside a generic class?

options.text: T must be abstract
Generics are only compile-time keywords for interfaces
Type erasure removes T at runtime
Java forbids arrays

explanation: Generics are erased at compile time, so the JVM does not know the actual type argument to instantiate.

stem: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?

options.text: O(log n)
O(n)

explanation: Each step halves the search range, giving logarithmic time.

stem: Reading an array element by index is:

options.text: O(n)
O(log n)

explanation: Arrays are contiguous, so the address is computed directly from the index.

stem: What is the time complexity of two nested loops that each run n times?

options.text: O(n)
O(2n)
O(log n)

explanation: n iterations times n iterations is n squared operations.

stem: What must every recursive function have to avoid infinite recursion?

options.text: A loop
A global variable
A return type of void
A base case

explanation: A base case stops the recursion, and each call must move toward it.

stem: Given a sorted array, which approach finds two numbers summing to a target in O(n) time and O(1) space?

options.text: Two pointers from both ends
Nested loops
Sorting again
Binary search for every element

explanation: Move the left pointer up if the sum is too small and the right pointer down if too large.

stem: A naive recursive Fibonacci `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` has what time complexity?

options.text: Linear, about O(n)
Exponential, about O(2^n)
Logarithmic, about O(log n)
Quadratic, about O(n^2)

explanation: Each call spawns two more with heavy overlap. Memoization reduces it to O(n).

stem: Which join returns only rows that have matching values in both tables?

options.text: LEFT JOIN
INNER JOIN
FULL OUTER JOIN
CROSS JOIN

explanation: INNER JOIN keeps only the matching rows from both sides.

stem: What is the main purpose of a database index?

options.text: Reduce the number of tables
Encrypt the data
Speed up lookups on the indexed columns
Enforce foreign keys

explanation: Indexes allow the database to find rows without scanning the whole table, at the cost of slower writes and more storage.

stem: Which query lists ALL customers, even those without orders?

options.text: SELECT * FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
SELECT * FROM customers c CROSS JOIN orders o WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN orders
SELECT * FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id

explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills missing right-side values with NULL.

stem: Which problem does normalisation primarily reduce?

options.text: Data redundancy and update anomalies
The number of characters in each query
The number of columns in every table
Network latency between the app and the database

explanation: Normalisation stores each fact once, which avoids inconsistent updates.

stem: A table has columns (student_id, course_id, course_name). course_name depends only on course_id. Which normal form is violated?

options.text: First normal form
Second normal form
Boyce-Codd is fine, nothing violated
Zero normal form

explanation: course_name depends on part of the composite key (course_id), which is a partial dependency that violates 2NF.

stem: Which query is LEAST likely to use an index on `email`?

options.text: WHERE email = 'a@b.com'
WHERE email LIKE 'a%'
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com'
WHERE email IN ('a@b.com')

explanation: Wrapping the column in a function typically prevents a plain index from being used unless a functional index exists.

stem: What does the @SpringBootApplication annotation enable?

options.text: Only the embedded web server and nothing else
Auto-configuration, component scanning and configuration in one annotation
A database connection pool with fixed settings
Automatic generation of REST controllers from entities

explanation: It combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan, so the app configures itself from the classpath.

stem: Which file holds the default configuration of a Spring Boot application?

options.text: pom.xml, which Maven reads when it builds the project
web.xml inside the WEB-INF directory
application.properties or application.yml
settings.gradle in the root folder

explanation: Spring Boot reads application.properties or application.yml for settings such as the port and datasource URL.

stem: Which injection style is generally preferred in Spring?

options.text: Field injection with @Autowired on private fields
Calling new on each dependency inside the class
Reading beans from a static global map
Constructor injection, which makes dependencies explicit and testable

explanation: Constructor injection lets you create the class in a test without Spring and makes required dependencies obvious.

stem: How can you stop a specific auto-configuration from being applied?

options.text: Exclude it with the exclude attribute or the spring.autoconfigure.exclude property
Delete the starter's jar from the local Maven repository
Rename the class that Spring detects at start-up
Comment it out of the JVM's boot classpath

explanation: Auto-configurations are conditional and can be excluded explicitly when they conflict with your own setup.

stem: A property is set in application.properties and also passed as a command-line argument. Which value wins?

options.text: The application.properties value, which always overrides everything
The command-line argument, which has higher precedence
The default value that is written in the code
Neither, because Spring refuses to start with duplicates

explanation: Spring Boot's external configuration order lets command-line arguments override files, which suits per-environment changes.

stem: Two beans implement the same interface and injection fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Which fix works?

options.text: Add @Autowired a second time to the field
Rename the interface so that Spring finds only one matching bean
Mark one bean @Primary or choose one with @Qualifier
Make both beans prototype scoped instead

explanation: Spring needs to know which candidate to inject. @Primary sets a default and @Qualifier picks one by name.

stem: Which status code means a resource was created?

options.text: 201 Created
204 No Content
304 Not Modified
400 Bad Request

explanation: 201 is returned after a successful POST that creates a resource, ideally with a Location header.

stem: Which URL best follows REST naming conventions?

options.text: /getOrderItems?id=42
/orders/42/items
/orders/delete/42/items
/doOrderItemsLookup/42

explanation: REST URLs name resources with nouns. The HTTP method says what to do with them.

stem: A client is signed in but lacks permission for an action. Which status code fits?

options.text: 401 Unauthorized
404 Not Found
403 Forbidden
409 Conflict

explanation: 403 means the server knows who you are and refuses. 401 means you are not authenticated.

stem: Which HTTP method is idempotent and replaces a resource entirely?

options.text: POST
PATCH
DELETE
PUT

explanation: PUT sends a full replacement and repeating it leaves the same result. PATCH changes part of a resource.

stem: Which change should force a new version of an API?

options.text: Removing or renaming a field that existing clients rely on
Adding an optional field to a response body
Fixing a typo in an error message's text
Improving the speed of an existing endpoint

explanation: Breaking changes need a new version. Adding optional fields is backward compatible.

stem: A PUT request is retried after a timeout. Why does idempotency matter?

options.text: It makes the request body smaller on each retry
Repeating the request leaves the same result instead of creating duplicates
It lets the server skip authentication on retries
It guarantees the first attempt was never received

explanation: Networks fail, so clients retry. Idempotent operations make retries safe.

stem: Which annotation marks a class as a JPA entity?

options.text: @Table on its own
@Component
@Entity
@Repository

explanation: @Entity registers the class with JPA. @Table only customises the table name.

stem: Which annotation marks the primary key field of an entity?

options.text: @Key
@Primary
@PrimaryKey
@Id

explanation: @Id identifies the primary key and is often paired with @GeneratedValue.

stem: What commonly causes a LazyInitializationException?

options.text: Accessing a lazy association after the session or transaction has closed
Loading an entity that has no primary key defined
Using more than one entity manager in the same thread
Mapping a collection with the wrong generic type

explanation: Lazy data is loaded on first access and needs an open session. Fetch it inside the transaction or use a join fetch.

stem: What does @Transactional do on a service method?

options.text: Makes the method execute on a background thread
Runs the method in a transaction that commits or rolls back as one unit
Caches the method's return value between calls
Encrypts the data written by the method

explanation: Either every change in the method is saved or, on a runtime exception, none are.

stem: What is the N+1 select problem?

options.text: N queries are merged into one by the database
A query returns N+1 duplicate rows for each parent
One query loads N parents, then N more queries load each parent's children
A table needs N+1 indexes before it can be queried fast

explanation: Looping over lazy children triggers a query per parent. A join fetch or entity graph loads them together.

stem: A @Transactional method calls another @Transactional method in the same class. Why may the inner settings be ignored?

options.text: Spring supports only one transaction per application
Inner methods always roll back the outer transaction
The inner method runs against a different database
The call bypasses the Spring proxy, so no new transactional behaviour applies

explanation: Transactions are applied by a proxy around the bean. A call inside the same object never passes through it.

stem: Which method starts a new thread of execution?

options.text: run()
begin()
execute()
start()

explanation: start() creates the thread and calls run() on it. Calling run() directly just executes on the current thread.

stem: Why use an ExecutorService instead of creating threads manually?

options.text: It reuses a managed pool of threads
It makes every task run faster than a single thread can
It removes the need to handle exceptions in tasks
It guarantees tasks finish in the order they were submitted

explanation: Pools avoid the cost of creating threads per task and put a limit on concurrency.

stem: What does the synchronized keyword guarantee for a block?

options.text: The block always completes within a fixed time
Only one thread at a time can run it for the same lock
Other threads can never read any of the variables used inside it
The block runs on the main thread only

explanation: synchronized gives mutual exclusion on a lock and makes the changes visible to the next thread that takes it.

stem: In which state is a thread that is waiting to enter a synchronized block held by another thread?

options.text: WAITING
TERMINATED
BLOCKED
NEW

explanation: BLOCKED means waiting for a monitor lock. WAITING is for Object.wait or join without a timeout.

stem: Two threads each hold one lock and wait for the lock the other holds. What is this called?

options.text: A race condition
Thread starvation
A memory leak
A deadlock

explanation: Neither can proceed. Acquire locks in a consistent order or use timeouts to avoid it.

stem: A fixed thread pool of 4 receives 100 tasks that each block on I/O for seconds. What is likely?

options.text: Tasks queue up, so throughput is limited by the 4 threads
Java automatically adds threads beyond the pool size
All 100 tasks run at the same time on 4 cores
The extra tasks are rejected straight away with a RejectedExecutionException

explanation: A fixed pool never grows and its queue is unbounded by default. Size the pool for the work, or use virtual threads for blocking I/O.

stem: In Spring Security, what runs before a request reaches a controller?

options.text: A chain of security filters
A set of database triggers
The embedded web server's logger
The JPA entity manager

explanation: Spring Security installs a filter chain that authenticates and authorises each request first.

stem: Which annotation restricts a method to users with a given role?

options.text: @Autowired
@PreAuthorize
@Transactional
@Scheduled

explanation: @PreAuthorize checks an expression such as hasRole('ADMIN') before the method runs.

stem: When is CSRF protection most important?

options.text: When the API only accepts requests that carry no cookies or tokens at all
When all endpoints are served over HTTP/2
When authentication uses cookies that browsers send automatically
When every response is cached by a CDN

explanation: Browsers attach cookies to cross-site requests, so an attacker's page can trigger actions. Header tokens are not sent automatically.

stem: Which component encodes passwords before they are stored?

options.text: A UserDetailsService that returns the raw password text
A SecurityFilterChain that hashes the URL
An AuthenticationEntryPoint that sends a 401
A PasswordEncoder such as BCryptPasswordEncoder

explanation: PasswordEncoder hashes with a salt and checks login attempts against the stored hash.

stem: What is the difference between hasRole('ADMIN') and hasAuthority('ADMIN')?

options.text: hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix, so it checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN
hasRole checks the HTTP method and hasAuthority checks the URL
They are identical in every configuration of Spring
hasAuthority only works with OAuth 2.0 tokens

explanation: Roles are authorities with a ROLE_ prefix. Using the wrong one is a common cause of unexpected 403 responses.

stem: Why is CSRF protection often disabled for a stateless API that sends a JWT in the Authorization header?

options.text: JWTs are encrypted so forged requests are impossible
Browsers do not attach that header automatically to cross-site requests
Spring cannot generate CSRF tokens for JSON requests
Headers are always ignored by the same-origin policy

explanation: The attack relies on automatic credentials such as cookies. A header the script must set itself is not sent by a forged form.

stem: What does an API gateway provide?

options.text: A shared database used by all services
A compiler for the services' source code
A backup copy of each service's logs
A single entry point that routes requests to the services

explanation: Clients call one address and the gateway routes, authenticates and rate-limits on behalf of the services.

stem: Microservices are best divided around what?

options.text: Business capabilities such as orders or payments
Technical layers such as controllers and repositories
The number of developers in each office
The programming language used in each file

explanation: Splitting by capability keeps related data and logic together so teams can change a service independently.

stem: What does an open circuit breaker do?

options.text: Retries the call again and again continuously until it succeeds
Fails calls fast without contacting the unhealthy service
Routes every call to the database directly
Restarts the unhealthy service automatically

explanation: After repeated failures the breaker opens and rejects calls immediately, giving the service time to recover.

stem: Why avoid sharing one database between microservices?

options.text: Databases cannot be accessed by more than one process
It makes every query slower than a network call
It couples services through the schema, so teams cannot change independently
It forces all services to use the same language

explanation: A shared schema means one team's change can break another service. Each service should own its data.

stem: Which concern is commonly handled at the gateway?

options.text: Business rules about pricing and discounts
Schema migrations for each separate service's own database
Compiling and packaging each service
Authentication, rate limiting and request routing

explanation: Cross-cutting edge concerns belong in the gateway, while business rules stay in the services.

stem: A service retries failed calls three times with no delay during an outage. What is the risk?

options.text: A retry storm that overloads the struggling service even further
The service recovers faster because it is warmed up
Retries are always blocked by the circuit breaker's closed state
Clients receive duplicate responses with no side effects

explanation: Immediate retries multiply the load on a failing service. Use backoff with jitter and a circuit breaker.

stem: What is a message queue used for?

options.text: Storing static files for a web server
Passing messages between services asynchronously
Compiling code in the background
Balancing incoming traffic between several data centres

explanation: A producer puts a message on the queue and a consumer handles it later, so neither waits for the other.

stem: In publish/subscribe, who receives a published message?

options.text: Only the first subscriber that connects
Only the publisher that sent it
Every subscriber of that topic
A random single subscriber each time

explanation: Pub/sub fans a message out to all current subscribers of the topic.

stem: A consumer crashes after reading a message but before processing it. How do brokers avoid losing the message?

options.text: Messages are copied to every consumer in advance
The producer sends the message again after a fixed delay of one day
Brokers keep no copy once a message has been read
Acknowledgements: unacknowledged messages are delivered again

explanation: The broker removes a message only after the consumer acknowledges it, so a crash leads to redelivery.

stem: What is a benefit of event-driven communication?

options.text: Services are decoupled because producers do not wait for consumers
Every service must know the others' addresses exactly
Events guarantee instantly consistent data everywhere
No message format needs to be agreed upon

explanation: Producers publish facts and consumers react, so services can change and scale independently.

stem: At-least-once delivery means consumers must be what?

options.text: Faster, because each message is guaranteed to arrive exactly once
Idempotent, because the same message can arrive twice
Stateless, because messages are never repeated
Single-threaded so that ordering is never lost

explanation: Redelivery after failures is expected, so handling a message twice must not cause a second side effect.

stem: Why partition a topic by a key such as order id?

options.text: To make every single consumer receive every event exactly twice
To avoid storing events on any disk
To keep related events in order within one partition
To let producers ignore the event schema

explanation: Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, so events for one order share a key and stay in sequence.

stem: Which annotation marks a JUnit 5 test method?

options.text: @Check
@Run
@Test
@Verify

explanation: @Test from org.junit.jupiter.api identifies a method as a test.

stem: What does Mockito's mock() create?

options.text: A copy of the real database connection and its open sessions
A thread that runs the test
A report of the code coverage
A fake object whose behaviour you control

explanation: A mock stands in for a real dependency so the class under test can be checked in isolation.

stem: What does when(repo.find(1)).thenReturn(user) do?

options.text: Makes the mock return user whenever find(1) is called
Saves user into the real repository permanently on every call
Verifies that find(1) was called exactly once
Throws an exception whenever find(1) is called

explanation: It stubs the mock's behaviour. Verification is a separate step using verify().

stem: Which Spring annotation starts the full application context for a test?

options.text: @MockBean
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
@Profile

explanation: @SpringBootTest loads the whole context, which suits integration tests. Unit tests usually avoid it.

stem: When is verify(mock, never()).send(any()) useful?

options.text: To make the mocked method return null
To count how long the method took to run in milliseconds
To assert that a side effect did not happen
To reset the mock before the next test

explanation: Verification checks interactions, including that something should not have been called.

stem: Which is a weakness of chasing 100% coverage?

options.text: Coverage tools slow every test down to about one test per minute
High coverage makes the production code run slower
Coverage cannot be measured for Java code
Tests can execute code without asserting anything meaningful

explanation: Coverage tells you what ran, not what was checked. Good assertions matter more than the percentage.

stem: Which instruction copies files from the build context into the image?

options.text: FROM
EXPOSE
COPY
ENV

explanation: COPY adds files to the image. FROM names the base, EXPOSE documents a port and ENV sets an environment variable.

stem: Why use a slim base image for a Java service?

options.text: Slim images run the JVM at double the speed
They allow running without a Java runtime at all
Docker refuses large base images in production
Smaller images pull faster and have fewer packages to patch

explanation: Less in the image means faster deployments and a smaller attack surface.

stem: What is the purpose of a multi-stage build for a Spring Boot jar?

options.text: Build with the JDK, then copy only the jar into a smaller runtime image
Run several copies of the application inside one container
Build the jar again every time the container starts
Share one layer between all images on the host

explanation: Build tools stay in the first stage and the final image holds just the runtime and the jar.

stem: What does an orchestrator do when a container crashes?

options.text: Stops the whole cluster until a person steps in
Restarts or reschedules it to keep the desired count running
Deletes the image from the registry
Moves the database into the container

explanation: Orchestrators compare the desired state with the actual state and repair the difference.

stem: Which ordering gives the best layer caching for a Maven project?

options.text: Copy all the source code first and fetch the dependencies afterwards
Run the tests before copying any files in
Copy pom.xml and fetch dependencies first, then copy the source
Fetch dependencies only after the container starts

explanation: Dependencies change rarely, so their layer stays cached while the source layer is rebuilt.

stem: A Spring Boot pod is killed with OOMKilled. What is a likely cause?

options.text: The pod's CPU limit was set too high for the node
The image was pulled from the wrong registry
The readiness probe returned a 200 status
The JVM heap plus overhead exceeded the container memory limit

explanation: The JVM needs memory beyond the heap. Set the limit above heap plus metaspace and thread stacks, or use container-aware heap sizing.

stem: What does a load balancer do?

options.text: Stores a copy of every database record
Spreads incoming requests across several servers
Compiles the source code before each new deployment starts
Encrypts the data stored on the disk

explanation: A load balancer shares traffic so no single server is overwhelmed and one failure does not stop the service.

stem: Why put a cache in front of a database?

options.text: To make every write instantly permanent
To replace the need for any database
To serve repeated reads faster and reduce database load
To keep the data private from administrators

explanation: Reads of popular data come from fast memory, so the database handles fewer queries.

stem: A health check fails for one server behind a load balancer. What should happen?

options.text: The balancer restarts the whole fleet of servers
All of the traffic is sent to the failed server to test it out
The balancer deletes the server from the account
The balancer stops sending it traffic until it passes again

explanation: Health checks let the balancer route around a failing instance, which keeps users unaffected.

stem: What is a read replica used for?

options.text: Serving read queries so the primary handles fewer reads
Accepting all of the writes whenever the primary is too busy
Storing the encryption keys for the primary
Compressing the primary's transaction log files

explanation: Replicas copy the primary's data and answer reads. Writes still go to the primary.

stem: What is the core difficulty of cache invalidation?

options.text: Caches cannot store anything bigger than one megabyte
Knowing when cached data is stale without losing the speed benefit
Caches always return data in the wrong order
Invalidation is blocked by most operating systems

explanation: Evict too late and users see old data. Evict too often and the cache stops helping.

stem: What is sharding?

options.text: Copying the same data to several read-only servers
Compressing old rows to save disk space on one server
Splitting data across several databases by a key such as user id
Running two databases as a primary and a standby pair

explanation: Sharding spreads both data and writes, at the cost of harder queries that span shards.
